Reading two billion stars

Astronomy × data at scale — the Gaia mission

Reading two billion stars
The Gaia toolkit, hands-on

ESA’s Gaia satellite measured the position, distance, motion, brightness and colour of nearly two billion stars — the largest, most precise map of our Galaxy ever made. From that one table you can do an astonishing amount of physics with almost nothing but arithmetic. This deck walks the three moves that define Gaia science — the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, finding star clusters by their shared motion, and measuring distances from parallax — each one live in your browser, then shown at a million-star scale.

A note on the data — the live archive isn’t reachable from this page, so the interactive parts generate a physically faithful synthetic catalogue on the fly (real colour–magnitude relations, a disk distance law, Gaia-like noise). Every relation is the true one, so the plots look and behave like real Gaia results. The embedded figures come from a 1,000,000-star run of the companion Python script.

The Contents menu (top), or Prev / Next (or ← → arrow keys), move through the pages.

What Gaia measures for each star

Everything here is built from six observables per star — nothing more:

Where it is

RA, Dec — position on the sky. Parallax ϖ — the tiny yearly wobble that gives distance.

How it moves

Proper motion (μα*, μδ) — how fast it drifts across the sky, in milli-arcseconds per year.

How bright

G magnitude — apparent brightness (smaller = brighter). Turns into intrinsic brightness once you know the distance.

What colour

BP − RP — blue minus red brightness; a direct proxy for surface temperature (blue = hot, red = cool).

That is the whole table. The art is combining these columns: distance from parallax turns apparent brightness into physics (the HR diagram), and shared motion reveals which stars were born together (clusters).

The cosmic ruler

As Earth orbits the Sun, a nearby star appears to shift against the far background — its parallax ϖ. The closer the star, the bigger the shift, and the relation is beautifully simple:

distance (parsec) = 1000 / ϖ (milli-arcsec) a star at 100 pc has ϖ = 10 mas; at 1000 pc, just 1 mas — Gaia measures shifts of microarcseconds

This is the first rung of the entire cosmic distance ladder: parallax calibrates everything beyond it. The catch is noise — parallax is tiny and its error grows for faint stars, so distances to far things are uncertain. That is why averaging many stars (a whole cluster) beats any single one.

Why it matters. Without distance, a bright dot could be a nearby dim star or a faraway brilliant one. Parallax breaks that degeneracy — and unlocks the HR diagram on the next pages.

Turning what you see into what a star is

Apparent magnitude m (what Gaia sees) mixes true luminosity with distance. Divide out the distance — via parallax — and you get the absolute magnitude M, the star’s intrinsic brightness on a common yardstick (as if placed at 10 pc):

M = m + 5 log10(ϖ / 1000) + 5 equivalently M = m − 5 log10(d/10 pc); brighter stars have smaller (even negative) M

Only once you have absolute magnitude can you compare stars fairly — and that is exactly what the vertical axis of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram needs. Colour (temperature) on one axis, absolute magnitude (luminosity) on the other, and the whole story of stellar physics falls out.

Parallax noise, made visible — because M uses the measured parallax, the noise on ϖ smears the faint end of the HR diagram. You will see that smearing appear naturally in the live diagram next.

The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, live

Plot every star as colour (x, temperature) versus absolute magnitude (y, luminosity) and something remarkable happens: stars don’t scatter randomly — they fall on sequences set by physics. Press Generate and watch a synthetic Gaia sample build the diagram in real time.

x: colour BP−RP (blue→red). y: absolute MG (bright at top). The dense diagonal is the main sequence; the branch upper-right is red giants (with the red-clump blob); the faint blue-left strip is white dwarfs. Coloured points are two star clusters tracing clean sequences.
What you are seeing — a star’s position on the main sequence is set almost entirely by its mass: hot, bright, blue, massive at the top; cool, dim, red, low-mass at the bottom. Giants have swollen after leaving the main sequence; white dwarfs are dead stellar cores. One plot, the life story of stars.

The same diagram, at a million stars

The live version above uses a few thousand stars so your browser stays smooth. Run the companion Python script over 1,000,000 stars and the sequences sharpen into the iconic Gaia image:

Density colour–magnitude diagram of the synthetic catalogue. Main sequence (dark ridge), the red clump and red-giant branch, and the faint white-dwarf cooling track (blue). Denser = darker.
Same code, more stars. Nothing changed but the count — the physics that draws the sequences is identical. This is the plot that, from real Gaia data, rewrote textbooks on stellar populations.

Star clusters — a shared birth

Open clusters are groups of stars formed from one cloud, so they share three things that make them findable in the Gaia table:

One distance

All members sit at essentially the same distance — so they share one parallax (a sharp spike, not a spread).

One motion

They drift together, so they share a proper motion — a tight clump in the (μα*, μδ) plane while the field scatters.

One age

Born together, so they trace a single clean isochrone on the HR diagram (you saw the coloured cluster sequences).

One patch of sky

Concentrated on the sky — though proper motion is the cleanest way to separate them from foreground/background stars.

The recipe. Select a clump in proper-motion space, and you have pulled a cluster out of a million field stars — then its shared parallax gives its distance to a few percent. That is the next widget.

Cluster recovery in the proper-motion plane

Each dot is a star’s motion across the sky. Field stars scatter in a diffuse blob around zero; a cluster, all drifting together, forms a tight clump that stands right out. Click “Select cluster A / B” — the members light up, and their shared parallax is turned into a distance on the spot, compared to the injected truth.

Grey: field stars (motion scattered about 0). Coloured clumps: two co-moving clusters. Selecting one gathers its members and computes distance = 1000 / median(parallax).
This is exactly how it’s done — real cluster catalogues (and membership lists) are built by clustering the Gaia proper-motion + parallax space. You just did the core of it.

A sharp spike among the crowd

Once the members are selected, their parallaxes pile up at one value while the field is spread across all distances. The median parallax gives the cluster distance to a few percent — here the million-star run recovers cluster A at 136 pc against the 136 pc injected:

Red: the proper-motion-selected cluster (a sharp parallax spike at ϖ = 7.35 mas). Grey: the broad field distribution. The dashed line marks the injected 136 pc.

And the proper-motion plane it was pulled from, at full scale:

The field blob at the origin with two co-moving clusters standing clear — the kinematic fingerprint of a shared origin.

Scale it up: an all-sky map

Give every star a place in a model Galaxy — an exponential disk threaded by two spiral arms, a central bulge, interstellar dust, and the Magellanic Clouds — and plot the detectable stars across the whole sky. The Milky Way draws itself:

Stellar density in Galactic coordinates (Mollweide). The bulge darkens at the Galactic centre; irregular pale gaps along the plane are interstellar dust; the two blobs below the plane are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds. Denser = darker.
This is the Gaia picture everyone knows — and it is nothing more than the same catalogue, every star placed by parallax and colour, counted per pixel.

Step out of the disk

The same stars, plotted in Galactic Cartesian coordinates instead of on the sky — a face-on and an edge-on view of the model Galaxy we are sitting inside:

Left: face-on — the disk and its two spiral arms, with the Sun marked at 8.2 kpc from the centre. Right: edge-on — the thin disk and the central bulge. Same catalogue, seen from the outside.

The whole sky drifts

Parallax gives distance; proper motion gives sideways speed. Because the Sun itself moves through the Galaxy, nearby stars show a systematic apparent drift — a clean dipole from the solar apex (the direction we head toward) to the antapex behind us:

Average reflex proper motion in each patch of sky. Arrows converge on the apex (orange) and stream out toward the antapex (blue), fastest at 90° between — a dipole Gaia measures directly. Darker = faster.
One catalogue, three views. The HR diagram is stellar physics, the all-sky map is Galactic structure, and this flow is kinematics — all from the same six numbers per star.

From a laptop toy to two billion stars

The live widgets use a few thousand stars; the figures use a million; real Gaia has ~2×109. The analysis doesn’t change — only the hardware does, and it is the same scale-out / scale-up story as any HPC problem:

Scale out (CPU / MPI)

The work is a pass over the star array — embarrassingly parallel. Split the rows across MPI ranks; each builds a partial 2-D histogram of the HR diagram or proper-motion map, then one Allreduce sums them into the global image.

Scale up (GPU)

Move the arrays to a GPU with CuPy or JAX; the histograms, colour transforms and selection cuts run on thousands of threads at once. A billion-row HR diagram in seconds.

And at catalogue scale, the query is SQL

You don’t hold two billion rows in memory — you stream them from columnar files (Parquet) and push the cuts and joins into a query engine. Selecting a cluster becomes one statement:

SELECT source_id, parallax, phot_g_mean_mag
FROM gaia_source
WHERE pmra BETWEEN 16 AND 24 AND pmdec BETWEEN -49 AND -41
  AND parallax BETWEEN 6.8 AND 7.9; the same proper-motion + parallax box, run by DuckDB / Spark-SQL over the whole catalogue
The through-line. Vectorise the physics, parallelise the pass (MPI across nodes, GPU within one), and let SQL handle the catalogue-scale I/O. Small toy, real method, Galaxy-scale ready.

What to carry away

  • Parallax is the ruler. distance = 1000/ϖ — the first rung of the cosmic distance ladder, and what turns apparent into absolute brightness.
  • The HR diagram is stellar physics in one plot. Colour (temperature) vs absolute magnitude (luminosity) sorts stars onto the main sequence, giant branch and white-dwarf sequence — essentially by mass and life stage.
  • Clusters reveal themselves through shared motion. A clump in proper-motion space, confirmed by a spike in parallax, is a group born together — and gives a distance good to a few percent.
  • It scales trivially. The whole analysis is a vectorised pass — MPI across nodes, GPU within one, SQL for catalogue I/O.
The companion code — gaia_showcase.py generates the 1,000,000-star catalogue and produces the three figures in ~3 seconds, with a note on the MPI/GPU scaling. Everything here is self-contained; the live widgets are a few hundred lines of JavaScript, no libraries.
